review_text_raw:
I love the game but it has some quirks.
1. Like some others, I believe that 'conflicting data chunks' should be revisable after entry pending new evidence.  The 'Test Case' has two personality traits that could both be true... or neither.  You have to choose one.
2. Is that... a bug?  Further into Test Case you need to find the full name of a Person of Interest.  I spent 10 minutes digging and digging through all available documents and found ONE listing of the name (immediately, actually) but it wasn't highlighted as a valid and usable Data Chunk.  Literally NOTHING else anywhere on this guy's name.  (Either I hardcore dumbed it up here or there's a bug regarding this Data Chunk.)
3. Restrictive Data Chunk gathering.  I recognized/found quite a bit of relevant data in documents but wasn't able to enter/drag-drop it as a Data Chunk into the appropriate Person of Interest's file... just because it didn't want me to worry about that yet?

Of course, I was just under an hour into the game and -mostly- (I think?) through the first 'Test' Case so issue #3 may just be a 'beginner' or tutorial-ish feature as it coaxes you into learning how to play without need of a cut-and-dry tutorial.  Overall, I say this game is definitely worth giving a try if you enjoy modern mysteries and actively uncovering the story for yourself.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
One of the game’s themes is how people present themselves online as well as offline. This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other in the game. Cassandra Watergate is, on one hand, an emotionally unstable, childish woman who does not care about adult responsibility, but on the other hand she is an activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police.

Which character is the real one? That is what makes the story interesting. Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are. People are different online and in the presence of other people. Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to make the player want to continue playing.

The gameplay itself is quite easy and straight-forward. You use Orwell to find data on various people supposedly involved in terrorist activities, in order to uncover who's responsible and who's not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue. Orwell might be easy, but that does not make it any less interesting. Simple, but very polished.

The game has an idea, but it gets repetitive quite fast. A 5/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]My playtime:[/b] 10h (based on steam, 100% achievement; 2.5x playthrough)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (17 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a massive information gathering system where you, an investigator, is taking a role in sorting the relevant data and fix conflicting data that the system gathered to assist a crime. The game has story branching that persists over 5 chapters.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 5 chapters
- Multiple endings and story branching that persists over the chapters
- Clean and fresh-looking interface
- You can restart a chapter after you finished the game

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Phone calls and chat animations take a very long time to finish
- Some clues are too hard to deduce unless if you know the full story
- You can't press the button to show conflicting data sometimes

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read or stalk people, you should buy this game. You also can buy it at a discount if you think that the playtime isn't worth the full price.[/i]

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The interface is clean and fresh-looking. I like how the summary that is shown at the end of the chapter is introduced; it looks like the workboard in my office except that it's way cleaner.

As someone who likes to try something by doing it firsthand, I don't find the design to be confusing. The portal section looks like your regular website, the message section looks like your regular chat app, and the device section looks like the simpler version of your device.

I'm also impressed by how the dev showed the photos; it looks like a fragmented version of our faces and it looks so detailed even though it's not. The important facial like eyes and hair is shown although most details are blurred and fragmented.

The cutscene at the prologue skipped a few frames to me though, although I don't have any trouble in understanding the story because of that.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story is being told by several conversations of your "adviser", someone who deduce things based on your findings, and whatever you read when you try to find clues, which are mostly from chat and phone calls.

Even though most conversations are held this way, I didn't find the main story to be confusing. Even if you couldn't understand the story, the "adviser" will give you some sort of info as to what is happening so you should be fine as long as you don't skip it. There's also a summary at the end of the chapter if you want to keep track of things.

There are several branchings in the game, either minor or major. I find the conversation between the branches to be smooth although some parts confused me since I didn't know the whole story at that moment. You need to play several playthroughs throughout the game to get all the major story branches and understand the whole story.

The thing is, there is no good or bad ending in this game; it's all about your opinion. You think what you think is good and bad. You also can deduce the whole story if you want or you can just understand the main story and be done with it.

[h1]The game[/h1]
[b]Features[/b]
There are 3 sections where you do most of your work: portal, message, and device. The in-game name is different, but I can't seem to recall the actual name since you don't need to know about the name to use it.

The portal consists of several web pages that you can access. The pages that you can access are limited to the system and more will show up as you unlock more clues.

The message, on the other hand, is a bit different. A message, either chat, email, or phone, will show up at certain times and you're allowed to wire-tap their chat and calls in real-time. The thing is, the chat speed is very slow. You can speed up the phone chat speed a bit although I still want it to be faster. It's taking too much time to listen to it especially when you're replaying your playthrough.

The device can be activated after you obtain a serial number of the target's device. You can access all files in the device, whether it's from a desktop or phone.

[b]Investigation[/b]
The suspect will have a profile page that you can fill with data. These data can be obtained by browsing through the 3 sections I mentioned. The data that you can take will be highlighted, either in blue or yellow.

Blue-colored means that there is no conflict with the data and yellow means that the data contradicts with other data. The game also has an option to show the conflicting data although I find that it's not working sometimes.

The thing is, you have freedom in choosing whatever you submit. I thought that I should fill all of the highlighted data in blue for complete profiling, but it's actually the opposite. All the data that you fill will be useful for the advisor's judgment and other people's fate, so you should decide carefully on what you submit.

Some data that you submit will change the story greatly, some are not. However, there are times where you have to make a major guess in determining the conflicting data that you must submit because you didn't know much and the clues are too vague at that point. Luckily, as I said before, there are no good and bad endings, so you can proceed as you please.

[b]Replayability and Length[/b]
As I said before, there are multiple endings. There are 5 chapters in total and each chapter except the last one lasts around 1 hour. I played the game fully twice and played one last playthrough from chapter 3 to unlock all of the major branching and achievement. It took me around 4 hours to finish all chapters at once.

Each chapter has a minimum of 2 endings that will affect the subsequent chapter. You can restart the whole story from the beginning or replay the chapter if you want after you finish the game once. Restarting the game from a specific chapter will delete all of the subsequent chapter data though.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
It's a nice game where you have to browse through things and wiretap people's communication to find out whatever is going on. The game has a lot of story branching and replayability.

review_text_raw:
[h1]The book 1984 by author George Orwell in a game. Splendid and intresting. While I've only read half of the book, I can still understand the connections. This must not happen in real life. I know it already does.. But we can still stop it..[/h1]
Ýou're yourself, a investigator with amazing spying tools. You get to spy on timelines, emails and even wire-tap phones.
You are looking for connections to put terrorists behind bars. The terrorists are bombing several buildings in Bonton, a fictional city in The Nation, a country where a Safety Bill has just gone through that puts investigators into control of the police work of The Nation. As a investigator for the law enforcement it is up to you to put the terrorists behind bars using Orwell. Orwell is a tool developed to find perpetrators before the crime is done. While there is flaws, terrorists and their groups are linked way faster than a human would think without the help of computers and social media sniffing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
10/10 Drag and drop simulator.

The game sounded really interesting but after 2 hours of playtime I refunded it. The idea that you hunt for information and decide what to pass on and what to keep private is a nice way of turning a game into a subtle reference to personal bias. A clever idea that could have been great. The problem is that, certainly for the 2 hours I played, that simply wasn't the case. There is no hunting for information. It is handed to you on a plate. The basic routine is this:

A page of information is loaded and appears on the right of the screen. Important parts of the text are highlighted. Click the highlighted text and drag it to the Orwell upload facility on the left of the screen. Drag enough pieces of text and a new page of information is presented to you with highlighted parts. Drag and drop. New page. Drag and drop. New page.

You will discover social media handles. Great, now you can hunt the person down and..oh wait, no their feed just gets presented to you with highlighted text. Drag and drop.

You manage to get the telephone number of a suspect. Now you can tap their line and listen in on their conversations. Oh wait, it just gets presented to you, no action required. Never mind, look, there's the symbol to say they are about to have a conversation. QUICK, check in and listen to them before they...oh wait, no. You can simply ignore the symbol for half an hour and then check it, because the messages only start when you open up the screen. If these really are terrorists, they are the most considerate ones on the planet as they refuse to start their conversation until you are listening in. Try to keep up? No need, go make a drink, come back and find the page of text. Ignore the drivel, the important bits are highlighted.  Drag and drop.

Still, your decisions about what to upload is really what the game is about. Except that even in those first 2 hours there were a few occasions where I decided not to upload something because it appeared to be out of context. A message displaying agressiveness or hatred of the state, but in the context of the document it seemed to be just social media waffle and not really genuine terrorist. So I didn't upload it. Result? Nothing. The game simply wouldn't progress until I uploaded it. The choice was removed. So after a while of hunting and finding no new clues I reluctantly uploaded the info and lo and behold a new page of information was presented to me. Drag and drop. Rinse and repeat.

Clearly a lot of people have found something great in this game and I truly love the concept but I cannot recommend it for what it claims to be.  If you are looking for the perfect Drag and Drop Simulator to spend your evenings on though, you can't go wrong here.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

[h1]Review[/h1]

 In Orwell you are an investigator, you need to investigate what might be a terrorist attack, and find the culprit(s). You can check people's background, access their emails, listen to their phone conversations or access their electronic devices. You can choose not to inform what you find to orwell or frame someone so he or she goes to jail.
 There are a couple of different endings, for both the story and the characters (including you, of course). Not all are happy.

[u]Why I liked[/u]
[list]
  [*] The Story: Is really rich, and depending on your choices, full of plot twists.
  [*] The Character Building: All the characters are really well written, how they interact between each other, and their personalities. I in part, what makes the story rich
[/list]

[u]Why didn't like[/u]
[list]
  [*] The UI/UX: You have an annoying companion, that cannot be disabled, that makes annoying comments about the data you upload. The uploading process could be faster also, I understand it tries to simulate a real computer connected to internet, but still it could be faster.
  [*] The Gameplay: Even though your choices matter, there are not a lot of choices you can make. All the data-chunks get highlighted, and the only options you have, are either uploading the information, or not. There's really no challenge, and probably by the third episode, you'll just be looking for highlighted text.
  [*] The replayability: I got all the Achievements in about 28 hours, and completed the game 4 times in that time, exploring all the endings.
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[h1]
 I thought I was going to find something different, something I could replay once and again. I really think the game has a lot of potential, but I can't recommend it.

review_text_raw:
[h1] How far are you willing to go to protect the populace? [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is a “visual novel” style game in which you have the ability to follow cyber-breadcrumbs in order to slowly uncover suspect’s online lives. Your goal? Stop a terrorist organization (?) from bombing public spaces. Your tools? As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

review_text_raw:
Stop what you're doing.

Stop reading this and buy the game. Now.

For 10 bucks? (I got it for 8 on sale though) This immersive experience is going to blow your mind (pardon the overused euphemism) but really. Wow. This was an absolutely fantastic ride. I do not regret spending my money on this game whatsoever! I think that, given some exposure on both Youtube and elsewhere, this game could get big! And it should! It's absolutely fantastic! I love the art style personally, but hey, that's personal taste.

Let me tell you precisely what you're getting so this review isn't just screaming praise about this game.

While the mechanics are beyond simple, (click various articles and search them for relevant data) it makes you feel really uneasy about delving into people's personal lives, about what it feels like to be in places you REALLY shouldn't be. 

All of the choices you make, each little piece of information you submit, can come back to bite you in the ass. Hard. If I have any tips for new players, don't just submit everything, ESPECIALLY conflicting data!!!! Make sure to read all bits of information and all of the articles in full before you submit everything! That's not just flavor text around the submittable parts, ALL OF IT IS IMPORTANT! And that's really what I like about this game- there's nothing gone to waste. Nothing that's just hopeless. All 'dead ends' are just waiting for the right door to open with another bit of text. It's nerve wracking and I LOVE it! 

I have no regrets on this game whatsoever. I'm more than happy that I bought it and I can't wait to see more (hopefully more excellent storytelling like in this game!) from the Devs. Really now, if you like story based games like the Telltale series of games, absolutely pick this up. What it lacks in mechanics it ABSOLUTELY makes up for in story, atmosphere, tension, and replayability! I'll be starting another playthrough shortly.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

review_text_raw:
[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality. [i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination. Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged. But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power. In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving. The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance. This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case? [i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it. Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down. /// [b]This review appeared on [url=https://kritiqal.com]Kritiqal[/url].[/b]

review_text_raw:
I expected to have to do more "detective work", but this is just a choices-don't-make-sense-but-they-matter experience.  Especially in the final chapter, I had little clue what I was supposed to accomplish, and then suddenly I accomplished something and the game was over.

If I could give this a Thumbs-Sideways, I would.  There are a few interesting "scenes" and moments that were surprising, but as it stands, I didn't feel like I was enjoying myself.  Just uploading "datachunks" and waiting for the game to find more datachunks to be uploaded.  Occasionally I had to decide between two conflicting pieces of data, but those choices were less-than-half of the game.  Maybe one-third of the game is "decisions" like that, and the rest is just dragging datachunks from one side of the screen to the other.  Or in some cases, deciding NOT to drag a datachunk from one side of the screen to the other, because it might be misunderstood by your superiors. For example, one comment on a website in-game says "oh no! the torture! ;)" in a playful manner about being bribed with muffins, but if you upload it your boss takes it to mean LITERAL TORTURE and freaks out about it.  So you're told to upload "all the relevant data" but then have no say in how it gets interpreted or used, which impacts upon the relevance of said data.

If you like games that try to make political-statements about things, this is probably up your alley.  I just wanted to solve puzzles, connect clues, etc.  The game highlights all the relevant information, and then connects it to things for you.  Not TERRIBLE, but not what I expected or hoped for. :(

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a rather close-to-the-bone spy em' up, not dissimilar to titles like Uplink in that they are set entirely in a digital, UI-based world.
Orwell has you performing surveillance on citizens of The Nation to ameliorate and defend against terrorist threats. 
The plot is compelling and is currently made up of five episodes, which altogether will take the average player around 2 hours to complete.
Unusual in it's gameplay mechanic, Orwell asks you to collate data about subjects (or targets) from the internet; using sites similar to Twitter, Facebook and blogs, you submit information to The Nation which allows it's security service to act. 
Information found and submitted is dependant on you, the human factor - decide to omit a vital piece of information, or include a misleading fact and you will influence what happens next.
This introduces some very difficult decisions and will test your ethical code. 

Orwell is highly reccomended - George would have been proud. Probably.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: This game comes from the same niche genre as Papers, Please, in which you operate as a government official tasked with keeping your country "safe" in a dystopian, high-surveillance world. It's a breath of fresh air in what I hope to be a more well-explored type of gameplay and setup. Instead of being the person to dismantle The System with guns a-blazing, you are a body warming your seat at a desk and following through with what your superiors ask of you--namely, monitoring and surveillance of certain individuals suspected of being involved in recent terrorist attacks in your country's capital. While many might find this to be a boring game, for us info-hunters and online archive fiends, this is exactly up our alley (and regardless, many people found themselves plenty surprised with how engaging Papers, Please was despite it being literal desk duty). The process of determining the relevant information from the chaff is an exercise in your detective work; conflicting bits of information challenges your ability to intuit context and intent, the results of your choices ultimately influencing the file you are compiling for your superiors, who can only draw conclusions based on it. Since they are depending on you to be diligent and honest, you are responsible for their ultimate decision on how to proceed at the end of the day. The interface is smooth, streamlined, and well-organized; your overseer Symes and his commentary on your findings is a tiny light in what would otherwise be a soul-sucking experience (at the end of the day, you are cutting your Persons of Interest into tiny bits of info); the music is an understated, mechanical heartbeat similar to Massive Attack's "Teardrop on Fire", famously used as the theme for the show House, M.D.. And at the end of the day, your choices matter. Only complaint is that sometimes your brain is thinking farther ahead than the game. There are several times when I thought "Wait, I remember who this is. I might as well jump on it upload a profile pic and the info from that file I found on them" but discovered I had to wait until the game found them relevant enough to devote any attention to them. I love this game and what it has to offer, and if anything I've said has piqued your interest, I pretty much guarantee you won't be disappointed.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A poignant game on the times we live in. I'm a humongous fan of the "Walking Simulator" genre and I stumbled upon this game during the Steam Winter Sale (3 days ago). Orwell has a captivating storyline that takes the "first person" experience quite literally. Without spoiling the game, the story focuses on a user operated software called Orwell, where the player assumes the role as a operator outside the fictatious "Nation", spying on activists that are tagged as potentially violent. 

The user interface is streamlined, dare I say "user-friendly". The fictional profiles depicted in the video game are unnervingly real, pulling me into the experience, as though as I really am spying on others. The characters are well scripted, albeit being scripts of text. The characters are caricatures of stereotypical activists, with complex backgrounds and hidden agendas. 

The "orwellian" connotations that are hinted at in the game are subtle, nuanced without being too overbearing or obvious. As you progressively submit information on labelled targets, you start to feel a heavy burden of responsibility on your shoulders. The multiple options and consequences from submitting false information add more weight to the situation. The activities or rituals performed by the main character are a frighteningly realistic, depecting the state of the world we live in. 

My only complaints include the duration of the game: it is rather short in length, more like a concept game showcasing some of the developer's strengths. The waiting times between each mission is abysmal, sometimes resulting in multiple crashes. 

All in all, this is an underrated gem in the walking simulator category, standing tall with the likes of Gone Home and Soma.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

review_text_raw: Orwell is basically just working but with more steps. Thankfully I got it on sale, but I wouldn’t recommend it as I felt I was just doing admin work the whole time. Osmotic Studios, a small German indie team, made this 2016 surveillance thriller where you play as a government agent using the Orwell system to dig through people’s emails, chats, social media, and documents after some incidents in a fictional country that feels a lot like a modern Western nation. You highlight and upload data, make choices about what goes into official reports, and watch the consequences play out. There’s a sequel too (Ignorance is Strength), which I've read is the same basic formula. Now the concept is clever on paper, digital Big Brother stuff inspired by the real world, and the writing tries to be thoughtful about privacy versus security.What I didn’t like: the actual gameplay is almost entirely reading walls of text, clicking highlighted bits, and filing them away. It starts feeling like busywork pretty fast, scrolling through inboxes, profiles, and logs for the next piece of info to stamp and upload. The interface is clean and the story has some twists, but the loop never evolves much beyond do your paperwork. It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
https://youtu.be/-dAXOFIVEDw

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This review won't matter much in the long run, but [i]Orwell[/i] just seems way over-rated to me. I'll try to explain why.

The story is needlessly convoluted, but let's set that aside.

The core gameplay mechanic (if you want to call it that) is dragging text from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. [b][u]That is all[/u][/b]: click to open windows to find text, then click and drag some portions of text that have been pre-selected and pre-highlighted as potentially relevant. When you drag text to the left side of the screen, it gets uploaded to the Orwell database as one of the results of your investigations. The Steam Trailer involves a bit of role-playing that doesn't quite represent gameplay accurately in this regard.

What really frustrated me was just how clumsy some of the most thematically important mechanics are. Sometimes, you find 2 "datachunks" of text (let's call them A and B) that conflict with each other, and you have to decide which one to upload. Your choice makes a difference to how the story unfolds, and affects people's lives. People can be arrested or die based on what you upload. The choices you make in situations like this constitute 100% of the moral complexity that [i]Orwell[/i] intends to confront you with. These decisions are central to the narrative, and to the player's experience.

Here's what's super lame: sometimes, when you find text A, and [i][u]before you could even possibly have an opportunity to see B[/u][/i]. the game says "A conflicts with [u]an unknown datachunk[/u]." This clumsy mechanic is in tension with the most basic plot-point of the game. The whole plot of the game is that The Nation needs [u]you[/u] to track down information and to decide what information goes into Orwell's databases. But what gameplay tells you is that [i]before you do anything[/i], Orwell already knows all the information that's out there, and knows when a conflict will arise, even when you (as the Investigator who is supposed to be influencing the story) have no idea yourself that B exists, and have done no detective work to suggest to Orwell that B exists. The whole thing is on (branching) rails, and your decisions amount to nothing more than selecting A vs. B, when Orwell can predict the conflict between A and B in advance. This means your detective work is essentially irrelevant; Orwell has done it all in advance, but won't share it with you. All that's left to matter is the choice between A and B.

One solution would've been to just let you resolve conflicts later: suppose that first you find and upload A, then later you find B, and you make a decision about whether to keep A in the database or replace it with B. But that would disrupt the game's ability to proceed with the narrative in a way that approximates a real-time unfolding of events. What the game wants to do is unfold the story as soon as you upload info to Orwell's database, irreversibly. If you upload A (whether or not you've seen B) then the A-chain of events begins. As a result, the game [b]has[/b] to tell you in advance that there's a conflict, so that you can "choose" which on-rails narrative will unfold.

So, my conclusion is that this is a game that is, fundamentally, poorly built. The core gameplay mechanics are kludges, patched together to facilitate the unfolding of the (branching) on-rails narrative. There are some choices to make, but the bulk of "investigative" gameplay is meaningless: this is a slideshow in games' clothing.
