review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
You've been selected to help the government of The Nation investigate and gather data on an activist group. You're to use their new mass surveillance software called Orwell.  Your job is to sift through all the data available to you, determine what is important, what is truth, and then submit this to the government.  If you do a good job, you could prevent future terrorism.

The gameplay is pretty basic, feels a lot like just browsing the internet and reading things.  You explore websites, chat logs, phone call transcripts, etc and you use the information within to create profiles on your subjects/targets.  The game tackles the opposing viewpoints on mass surveillance, asking questions like - is it ok to spy on citizens for their own safety even if it's at the expense of some civil rights?  And where does this end?

I really liked the characters in this game, they felt very real to me.  Each with their own personalities, motivations, realistic reactions to the events of the world around them.  The dialogue was interesting to read too, though I felt it sometimes moved along a bit too slow.  I enjoyed digging deep in each person's life, trying to determine their guilt or innocence.  I really liked that the game allowed me to impact events.  I could submit data that would lead to a person's arrest.  I could paint the portrait of events to wrongly accuse someone, or I could save lives by taking a terrorist off the streets.

The game has 5 chapters and took me a little over 5 hours to beat.  Once you've beaten it, a recent patch allows you to go back to any previous chapter to replay it and do things differently if you wish and see how things play out.

I do wish the game was longer.  I wish it allowed me to explore more narratives than simply one activist group's possible involvement in terrorism.  But for what it is, I still liked it immensely and fully recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Ultimately, my review comes down to one question:  "Would I pay for this?"  The answer is, no I don't think I would.  I can certainly see where this game would appeal to some, but it doesn't to me.  Hence, the negative score.  I don't regret playing it for free, but I don't think I would have been missing out had I not played it.

Orwell is a story game, first and foremost.  It has somewhat non-linear story to tell, where your actions will affect the details of the plot, but it'll otherwise run more or less the same, and you'll have a choice of three or four endings depending on how you do the finale.  The game tries to cover the problem of survellience but... IMO, it misses the mark completely when the tools used to spy are... indept.  More on that later.

The game boils down to reading fictional internet pages, spying on emails, calls, and texts, and snooping on people's computers.  Your goal is to find "important" information, that is pre-highlighted for you, and drag and drop what you feel is important.  The game stresses that you try to pick correct and relevant information but, ultimately, there's no failure state.  Being accurate or inaccurate only affects the plot details, nothing else, and kinda underminds the engagement of what little gameplay there is.

There's major problems with this though.  You're an investigator on a case, but your partner and the tools you're using are inept.  You can supply information, but you're often not allowed to include the context too.  Context is stupid important in real investigations, so it really undermines, well, the whole system.  You'll also come across "conflicting data", sometimes before you've even found the info it conflicts with.  A good investigator would record it all and then review it later and dismiss what's incorrect.  In Orwell?  You have to pick one.  And sometimes you have to pick blindly.  Just... why?  You also cannot collect information on individuals related to the main suspects, something I figure would be rather important.

It'll also leave you wondering one major question:  what sort of security and surveillance dystopia doesn't even have basic information, such as dates of birth and known addresses, already on file?  For a government trying to imitate 1984's Big Brother, they're failing hard at it.  Especially when around 75% of the information you're gathering is from public sources...

This here's the whole problem:  the game tries to make you question whether government observation is good or bad and whether things should be more private.  But then it puts you in the role of a guy who spends a lot of the time collecting publicly posted information and digging up stuff slower than a Google search.  Snooping into calls, computers, and bank accounts is certainly fishy, yeah, but nothing that would be legally off-limits to a police officer with a warrant in Real Life™.  And considering the plot... warrants are totally justified for everyone involved.

Orwell tries, and the story is just interesting enough for a 3-4 hour playthrough.  But... the political discussion just falls flat due to its own gameplay.  And there's games that are much better at hunting down and acquiring your information without highlighting it for you, like the parts of Hacknet focused on snooping.  

IMO:  not really worth the buy.  If you're really curious, try the demo and if you still want it, wait for a sale.

review_text_raw:
Worth it? Yes. DLC? Yes. Get it on sale? Probably, but it's worth the price if you have disposable income.
I really enjoyed playing Orwell and its DLC. Here's a bullet point of stuff I think is worth knowing before you buy!

-Plot/characters are realistic in a way that would normally be mundane on their own, but this game makes it somehow feel exceptional enough to make the story worth investing in. I think this grounding to reality did a good service by this game's namesake to express the urgency and importance of privacy and compassion, IRL and online.

-Easy to navigate UI, text is usually easy to read. The news articles' text is a bit thin, but if you have a big monitory/screen it probably won't be a problem. And you typically don't need to read every word on each website and email anyway.

-Markers for unread/unused/new "datachunks" that make going back through old info much less tedious.

-Easy to immerse in because you don't have to pretend to be someone you're not to fit yourself into the world of the game. It does feel like a job, but one that has wild stuff happening and your only way to know about it is through the job. Making the player curious is really important for mystery/puzzle/investigative games, and this game did a 7/10 job with that.

-While it does take effort to make sure you're keeping up with all the info, and making sure you're not wasting resources on unimportant info; it's not overly difficult. it's not necessarily easy (the first time around), but it won't make you feel stupid if you do struggle.

-The general concept of this game is so cool to me, I wish there were a lot more games like this.

-This game is much more accessible to people who have little in-depth experience with technology. It does all the technical "hacker" type work for you, and just lets you dig through people's lives unburdened. I don't really care about all the technical stuff involved in hacking & the like, so this was a huge win for me. A game like this can flop because of poorly executed, insanely difficult to comprehend, or super unrealistic hacking mechanics; so Orwell pretty much bypassed that while still making you feel like you're putting the pieces together yourself. (As long as you don't think too hard about it, anyway.)

-It puts you in a position of being the bad guy in a situation that makes you think, "This could literally be happening IRL and I wouldn't know." This game will give you a lot to think about even after you're done playing. 

-There is an issue that happened to me twice, where I technically soft locked myself in the game, and was unable to find any answers through walkthroughs/watching others play the game. So be prepared to be very diligent when uploading info when you are not racing the clock, and don't log out for the day until you're absolutely certain you've nabbed all the important info you might need.

-This game is honestly a bit short for the sheer amount of story and world-building information available in it. I think the game should have given you more time to explore and given more options for gathering info before forcing the plot to continue, even if not all of the info is used. It holds your hand too much, but not outright.

-Overall, my biggest issues with this game have to be the fact that you can't skip or pause chats or phone calls you're observing, and it moves so fast at certain points that you don't have time to process the information you're gathering to learn about the world/characters/story. My favorite parts of this game are really just the overall experience of playing it, and the execution of concept being very clear and deliberate.

review_text_raw:
[b]Pros[/b]
+60FPS
+Good story
+Investigation was fun
+Interesting low polygon art style
+Clean UI
+Soundtrack

[b]Cons[/b]
+Lots of hand holding
+Several bugs (one big one hovering over datachunks)
+Phone calls and texts take too long to finish

An interesting game that has you in control of a “Big Brother” surveillance system named Orwell. You must find out who or what is behind several violent attacks on a city. As you go through the story you must upload information you deem important (or fake info to throw Orwell off). Emails, texts, phone calls, computers, websites, etc. it’s all available to search through and piece the puzzle together. There is a lot of reading, but the info you can upload will get highlighted automatically. Sometimes there are conflicting pieces of information and you’ll need to decide what to upload.

The story is good with some twists and turns. It does have several endings and outcomes depending on your choices throughout each day. The gameplay is very straightforward and you can dumb it down to dragging things from one side of the screen to another until things happen. If you get into the game, it feels more than simply drag and drop. I found myself pausing and thinking things through, second guessing, regretting some uploads, etc. 

I did come across a rather annoying bug which seems to be common when looking at the discussions. Seemingly at random, when you hover over a highlighted piece of information it will not show you the summary of what gets uploaded to Orwell. This is a huge bummer because then you are uploading information that you may think one thing but the game thinks another. Sometimes logging out and going to the main menu fixes it, but not always. 


[b]Conclusion[/b]
I went back and played through it a second time to see different outcomes and to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed my time with the game and would recommend it on sale.

[b]6/10[/b] Above Average

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Much less a game than an interactive story. It's a slim game with few objectives and a lot of fluff around it. The game tends to cram exposition into everything, and doesn't allow you to skip or fast-forward any of it. Utimately, while the plot is about making a god of machines, it doesn't justify its deus ex machina storytelling.

[h1]Show, Don't Tell[/h1]
I do not know who's idea it was to not allow the player to fast-forward or skip dialogue, but it was a [b]terrible[/b] decision. The sheer amount of exposition and meaningless chatter in the game is astounding. And this isn't a once or twice occurance, it's a regularly reoccuring situation where key bits of info required to advance the plot sit behind a 4 or 5 minute long unskippable dialogue sequence. And that 10+ minute bit right before the end of the game, who thought that was a good idea? And does the "administrator" need to say something every time I upload a piece of relevant info? It's like having Clippy from MS Word permanently built into the game.

Furthermore, the level of hand-holding is ridiculous. First off, for a game about parsing and collecting information, there's very little you actually have to read. The game essentially takes a big neon highlighter and highlights every single thing that might be of importance. Then, they go ahead and show you exactly where you might've missed a clue or hint. Secondly, the game has these "pivotal" moments where you have to decide which one of multiple conflicting statements is true, except that the system highlights conflicts before you even discover them. It's such a self-defeating mechanism. Imagine if the Sherlock novels had Watson discover a false clue and Sherlock responding "But Watson, that can't be the real clue cause I'm going to find the real clue on page 86!"

And if the story was entralling, and the world-building was coherent, maybe those bad gameplay elements could be overlooked. But they aren't. The plot is cheesy and the writing is lazy. How many times do you plan on having a random character with no background conveniently appear to tie-up some loose ends and then disappear forever? It's honestly kind of amazing how a game where everything you do is character building manages to have some of the most one-dimensional characters I've ever seen.

[h1]Breakdown[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Chapter Select:[/b] Thanks for at least not making me have to replay the whole game to get an achievement.
[/olist]
[b]Cons[/b]
[olist]
    [*][b]Don't stop users from fast-forwarding text.[/b]
    [*][b]Narrative, not Narrate:[/b] I should be able to tell when I come across an important piece of dialogue. I don't need the game to highlight it a bright color, the music to change to be all dramatic, and Clippy at the top exclaiming, "Wow! That piece of dialogue sure seems important!" *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge*
[/olist]
[b]Score[/b]: 2/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'll admit, I was skeptical, even with all the glowing reviews on Steam. However, bored with playing the same old games, I decided to give the game a try since it wasn't even 10$. As I started up the game, I asked myself - how this game could possibly keep me interested? It's a game where you're literally staring at a 'computer' screen in-game.. when you're already staring at a computer screen in real life. Not even 10 minutes in and I was hooked. I needed more information and I needed it NOW! I got really invested in the fictional characters stories, lives and background; why did she break up with him? How long were they dating? Why is 'X's relationship with her parents so strained? I looked through every single e-mail and chat message I could find. I listened to countless phone calls and actually cared what was said and listened intently. All the while snickering to myself because the fictional characters didn't know I was listening in on their conversations. 

This game proves that sometimes being innovative and creative pays off. The game was worth every last dollar. It's relatively short (6 hours) and  I played all the episodes straight through, but it still managed to keep me excited and interest throughout the whole game. I kept playing 'just 10 more minutes' to find new information. Although only 6 hours long, I felt like it's the perfect length. Any longer and I probably would have started getting annoyed (because I did want to find out the ending to the story). 

The only issues I had with the game was that it doesn't really explain how the 'upload information' works. It tells you very briefly what your job is - to upload information, but I didn't understand that I could literally choose what information to upload and what to withold. I thought I had to upload certain information to continue with the story - turns out that may not have necessarily been the case. I actually got an ending I didn't intend because even at the end of the game I wasn't really sure what I was supposed to be doing (how did I access information, not upload it but still continue with the story?). You would think 'upload information' would be an easy concept to understand and wouldn't really need a tutorial, but in my case I would have liked a proper 2-3 minute introduction to how Orwell 'works'. The fact that you can choose what you do and do not upload, and depending on that - there will be different concequences. 
The highlighting of relevant text kinda made the game too easy, but I do understand the necessity of the function. Any real-life program such as Orwell would probably have a similar feature that highlights relevant information. I felt like it made the game more realistic because occassionally while reading an on-going chat, I could quickly scan for relevant information that was highlighted - upload it - and then continue reading the conversation. 
I really idn't realize that my actions of uploading certain information would have concequences; I guess I thought the game was a lot more linear, not that I could actually influence what happened by what I did or did not upload. 

This was really unique, both in game-playstyle as well as story telling. I'll be playing it again, that's for sure.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The Gameplay:
The style of gameplay is certainly unorthodox from your standard games, but it is easy to understand and even empowering. You essentially link relevant information regarding a person or event and depending on how you do that, certain events will play out.

The Story:
You operate a special hacking suite provided by the government to pry into someone's life and essentially build a report about the person and their activities. There is person receiving your report and they act on what you provide. It was interesting to follow and felt real enough to hit home a lot of times. 

The Visuals:
The art choice was interesting for the characters giving them a somewhat pixelated look. The actual HUD was very nice to look at and easy to use. 

The Sound:
The soundtrack was distinct and set a nice atmosphere for the work you are about to do. Nothing else really stood out save for some of the menu noises which were neat. 


The Experience:
When getting this game, I thought I would find it mildly entertaining. I was not prepared for how into the game I would end up getting. I was so enthralled with the way the investigation pans out that I got a notepad and started jotting down relevant info and dates to make sure I could solve the case. 

It has a decent amount of replayability since you can choose different options which very satisfyingly changes the context of the rest of the story. The game hit that sweet spot of not being too short nor being too long. Overall I feel Orwell did a good job of putting you in the seat of the Investigator and keeping the game and story fresh.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really wish I liked it because on the paper it's 100% a game for me but I'm forced to admit I just don't.

First of all it's not detective work, you just drop pieces of information in a database hoping it makes the story progress.

Because you're not technically forced to drop all the information in the database, you quickly try to have an impact on the story's progression by keeping some info to yourself, but the story only progresses when specific info is used and you never know which info is necessary or not so you can't really make informed choices on what to give Orwell and what to not.

I quickly find myself stuck with the story not progressing because I've decided to keep a piece of information that's mandatory for the story to continue and so I have to start from the top and review everything which is tedious and drop random bits of information I've kept until I find the one that was necessary for the story to continue which means I really can't choose what I keep or don't keep,

or I straight up give all the info away from the start to not have to review everything later once I'm stuck which again means I can't choose what I keep or don't keep.

There seems to be a system of highlighting the files where there still is relevant information but I don't understand how it works. Sometimes files are highlighted and there's nothing left on them and sometimes they aren't highlighted and there's still important things on them. It's very confusing.

I also suspect the political messaging of the game is really not so subtle and just "violence is bad" with no nuance but I can't tell you for sure because I'm too frustrated with the gameplay to go to the end of the story at this point. My other issue with the writing that I just can't seem to get over is that it makes zero sense that people who are fighting surveillance would post on the internet about it with their full name and photo or extremely basic aliases. Not posting about your actions on the internet is activism 101.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
GENERAL OVERVIEW
Awesome game and "out-of-the-box" genre. Gameplay is very interesting since you analyze the suspects from a digital device, without physically following them. You get to know every small aspects of their lives, but this is a factor that greatly complicates the developer's work. For the ones who love the detective genre, this one is a very good choice. But I can't give a fully positive opinion on this: let's start with the upsides.
PROS
1)Rich and deep story. Keeps the gamer interested.
2)Orwell system is very well structured, its display is simple and not effort-requiring.
3)Plot-twists excluded, the game is actually chill. It keeps you concentrated, but not nervous or stressed. The fact that you can sit down and think of your next move, gives the game the right pace.
CONS
1)Low graphic and audio impact. Although the story keeps the gamer focused, that is probably the only one factor. I dare to say the game has a poor multimedial content. Characters don't "say" a single word for all the story.. You just hear music and other minor sound effects.
2)Too often it remains unclear where "the game finishes and the gamer starts". Has it ever happened to you that you can't understand how heavy will your decision be on your remaining gameplay? It happens too many times in Orwell. It's not clear when your action will bring to irreversible consequences, and this is annoying. Sometimes it feels like the game is playing you, and this is boring because the plot does not prompt the player to take important actions.
3)Insufficiently exhaustive tutorial. Although Orwell is pretty much a game with a "simple dynamic", basically gathering relevant information, I think that the small tutorial in the beginning does not clarify enough what the Orwell system is about. Even though in the tutorial-phase of the game is explained how you should deal with Orwell, the gamer fully grasps the concept after some time, and this is not acceptable in a game where choices matter (especially in one where it's not clear where choices are supposed to be made!). I came from hundreds of detective-genre games but this one is different, the developer knows, so maybe they should have stressed the basic principle more.
4)Lack of languages. This is a text-adventure. There should be plenty of available languages! I understand that this would be an incredibly long job... But this is a noticeable downside. This is quite a problem for non-natives english speakers, and a barrier for non english speakers.
5) You gather information on this system called Orwell, but as you go on with the game, you may find out more precise details, or that the information you considered relevant are just circumstancial. This is a normal day in the life of an investigator. So, why can't the player modify the datachunks relating to characters' pages? this is a forcing. A super complex system like Orwell doesn't allow the investigator to cancel what he wrote?
OVERALL OPINION
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a very nice game, that will be appreciated by most of the detective-games community. It's passionating, you would never desire it to end, it makes you feel a real investigator. Nevertheless, it has noteworthy downsides and there's a wide improvement margin under some aspects. Recommended.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This review doesn't contain spoilers:

This is a brilliant game! I've never played anything like it before and now I'm interested in buying the next season in the series.

Simple Plot: Basically you play an intelligence agent tasked to investigate the events around a terror attack in a fictional country that's run by an Orwellian government. 

Gameplay: Text based but accompanied by rather interesting visuals and calm music. Your character (basically you) can monitor citizens computers, phones, bank accounts etc secretly, while building profiles for them and submitting data you think is incriminating up to your bosses. There's a lot of skimming through data, but it's worth it because you start unravelling a storyline and secrets people hide from each other. You're basically playing something like a simulated intelligence agent screen. There are 5 days which will take about 6-ish hours to complete the game if you play nonstop.

Graphics: Smooth and nice but it doesn't really take up much to generate the graphics in this game as much of the game is texts and chat boxes. The art style of people are picasso-ish and there's only one animated scene at the beginning of the game.

Value: I've never played any kind of text based game before so this opened up a whole new world of experience for me! I really enjoyed it so I felt it was worth it! The other thing is that there are multiple endings you could choose so you can replay the game several times to choose different endings. Achievement hunting is rather easy and doesn't require much skill but rather to make different choices in the game.

7/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there were a rating between recommended and not recommended. Like a 'Eh, maybe?' option.  This game is very well designed with a great UI and intuitive progression. You do make some decisions and those decisions do have a pretty big impact on the story, but that is also where the bulk of my criticism comes from.

The decisions that make a huge difference feel incredibly arbitrary, so instead of feeling like you're investigating and making decisions, it feels like a game of guessing what the *developers* want you to do. It also railroads you into things I don't agree with and wouldn't choose to do, but if you don't do them you get stuck or really bad things happen. The guy you interact with (your point of contact) is very volatile and makes weirdly intense decisions off of very limited information, which can entirely screw up your game if you're going for the best results for everyone involved and it can be really hard to tell when he's going to do that. 

Initially I tried to play cautiously, withholding information I felt could be abused, and that ended up with people dying. So I quit where I was and restarted the whole game (boring, because this game is not very replayable) and had to try a few times before I figured out exactly what was causing the issue. Then I thought I better understood the game so I continued, only to find that I gave *too much* information to them which resulted in more deaths. 

It just doesn't feel like a game where the goal is about making the *best* decisions, it feels like a game where the goal is making whatever decisions the devs want you to make, and that's too much random guesswork to be fun for me. I stopped playing after Chapter 2 because I was tired of trying to read their minds.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intro:

 Eric Arthur Blair (famously known under the pen name of George Orwell) was a essayist (someone who writes essays for a living), novelist, critic and journalist.  He lived between 25th of June 1903 to 21th of January 1950 and was most famous for two books.  Namely Animal Farm (17 August 1945) and 1984 (8 June 1949).  Animal Farm is considered to be a classic of allegorical story-telling and political satire. 1984 on the other hand is a book where endless parallels can be drawn to in real life. 

Where the grim (sometimes terrifying) warnings of totalitarianism, twisting of words, meaning and history appear to become more of an reality.  1984 is considered to be one of the best books ever written (an opinion that I share myself).  Its influence on narrative art, politics and language cannot be understated.  Today’s game: Orwell owes a lot to 1984, right down to naming itself after Blair’s pen surname.  

Story:

One of the game’s themes and commentary is how people present themselves online and “offline”.  This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other.  Cassandra Watergate (get it?!) is on one hand,  an emotionally unstable, childish woman who  does not care about adult responsibility.  However on the other hand she is apparently a activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police. 

Which character is the real thing? That is what helps make the story compelling, Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are.  People are very different online and in the presence of other people (could this man be impersonating another man who might not even be alive?!).  Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to compel the player to continue playing. 

Gameplay:

Gameplay is rather easy and straightforward.  You use Orwell to find data on various persons supposedly involved in terrorist activities. In order to uncover who was responsible and who was not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue.  At worst you have to decide which information is relevant to which character.  You would also have to decide what information is important or valid (someone saying that they are from wonderland is not valid for obvious reasons).  However there is not much of a failure (at least for me )  as all I got was a scolding from Symes.  However I did find myself debating on the various behaviour patterns and deciding which behaviour fits with the character’s overall personality. Orwell might be easy but that does not mean it is not compelling.  Simple but straightforward and very polished. 

Conclusion:

Orwell’s relevance is undeniable, the balance between private and public with the invention of Social media has become.  The encroachment of government surveillance for safety from a threat that might not exist is a legitimate possibility.  The erasure of privacy encouraged by the likes of Facebook and Twitter. Where everything you say and do is recorded to be sold to the highest bidder.  Orwell’s importance as a game will always be relevant while Britain and China’s surveillance states continue to become more of a reality.

review_text_raw:
ohh this is really, really well-done. To a large extent, this is what I've always wanted from a mystery game: being able to/having to think and reason for yourself, draw conclusions, then have them reflect in the game - rather than being taken through a sequence of 'revelations' by the game plot. Partially reminds me of old-school RPGs that didn't write down all the relevant information in the quest log for you and/or spell out the revelations and point you in the right direction - you had to put two and two together yourself. I actually took notes playing this game!

Things that made it a good mystery-like experience: Having to make judgement calls based on incomplete information. Occasional moments of adrenaline rush as you make genuinely (as far as I can tell as a player, anyway) time-sensitive calls. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I really want to like Orwell for the principle of trying to deliver a social media exploitation simulator, but ultimately, it's a flow-chart puzzle that only allows the player to progress once he or she has collected the necessary datachunks. This would be unobtrusive if the narrator (the guide) wasn't hovering over you at all times like an incompetent manager - instantly responding with positive or negative feedback. The game would be much better if you could upload information to something like a holding pool to review as a whole before submitting it to something like a file or record for the manager to review, but instead, the game flow pauses and continues with no continuity of real-time, even though the game desperately tries to emulate this moment of your day on the job . You might have a hunch about a suspect as you read information, so you would think to point out correlated characteristics, but nope, that doesn't matter because you can only upload information the game has already marked as valid.

Orwell is unique and immersive, so it does have that going for it, but the flow-chart progression heavily relies on the game being bug free. I hit a bug/glitch/design flaw in the second episode in which a datachunk in the suspects relationship field was not registering that I uploaded it. As a result, I was stuck. I poured over every bit of information for about three hours before I finally searched online for help and wound up uploading conflicting datachunks to do what I thought would fail the mission, but oh, how convenient, the game saves the day by holding my hand and progressing anyway. So, it’s more like an interactive novel than a social-engineering investigation simulator.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This was a very enjoyable little game, and pretty fairly priced at just £7. I found it in an article in PC Gamer magazine and decided to give it a go, being a big fan of George Orwell's strong writings myself. This game is surprisingly tense and fast paced at times, while at other times the story can be kind of slow. The thing is, this game shows the player the whole "Big Brother State" issue from the other side, you get to see reports of terrible events you could have stopped and it really hit me very hard.

This is a game that has obviously taken real events into consideration as much as Orwell. The undertones in The Nation and the leadership by The Party feels like it would work well as a prequel to one of Orwell's most famous works, Nineteen Eighty-Four, which was so influential it even got a big screen adaptation and starred a great cast for the time including a very young John Hurt. But I digress. The storyline is based around a crowd-surveilance computer interface called Orwell and is brought about in secret after The Party passes the Secrecy Bill. I won't spoil anything about the investigation, but the Bill is very reminiscent of British PM Theresa May's highly controversial Snooper's Charter.

The fact is, the game has this utopian near-future look while having tense feelings of underlying political risk to every act. The five chapters work pretty well to split them up, and the way the interface works is really nice. Every part of the investigation manages to have a consequence, but it leads to the same kind of point in the end. So, in Conclusion:

Pros:

1) Excellent storyline with strong characters and some really tense chapters, such as Nina's storyark (that was both intense and really threw me off, again one you'll have to see for yourself) and the antics of Initiate.

2) An interface that really makes you feel like the investigator.

3) Attention to detail - the game doesn't hold back with its attempts at realism.

4) A real feeling of influence and a concern that this game may be showing the future.

Cons

1) The lack of potential for follow-on sequels - The game ends on a sort-of final note, as you'll find out if you play it.

2) CCTV or Camera Footage actually plays very little part in the game, with text being very dominant. Would be nice have to access event footage, more access to records in the hands of actual authorities and the like to even out the fact it is a government project, not a bedroom-hacker.

3) The length of the game could be greater, If a longer sequel appeared I would certainly want to buy it!

4) Finally, the route taken is too narrow. This game is meant to show the full potential and range of issues a Big Brother style investigation would have, so more routes for different events would create greater depth and realism, as well as adding replayablity.

So, I thoroughly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys a good who-done-it with a political/ sci-fi twist. 100% a decent little game!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game feels like a visual novel. You are in charge of gathering information on different suspects of a terrorist attack with the help of Orwell a software that gather information from social media, phone calls, emails...

Pros:
Good story and concept.
Great Design
Shows how easy it is to make a profile of someone from what you can gather on the internet

Cons:
Lack of real choices or intelligent ones. The software preselects whatever information you want to add to the suspects profiles and forces you to choose between "conflicting" information, but an individual thoughts are not black or white. Most people tweet stuff that they regret later or that do not represent there views...
Bugs. The software sends you notification to read new information and add it or not to the profiles, but sometimes it doesn't work. Either doesn't show a notification or notifies you of something you already read or already added to the profile. Which leads, sometimes to reread every piece of information to find the one entry you missed in order to continue to the next chapter.

After a couple of hours I felt it was not very enjoyable to hunt for new information or get blocked on a chapter for a while even though the game tells you that you can omit to upload information to the suspect profiles...
I still think it is a great idea but they should leave more decisions to the player and don't block the player from continuing through the story. If the player didn't find enough evidence than he will not find the culprit --> Game over rather than be stopped from advancing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.
